teacher_raw:
<STATEMENT>
# Problem A — Sealing a Facility into Isolated Containment Zones

Time limit: 5 s   Memory limit: 256 MB

## Description
A research facility is a network of $n$ rooms joined by $m$ corridors, each corridor carrying a sealing cost that reflects the labour and materials to close it permanently. Several rooms (guaranteed to be at most $n$ in number) are designated containment sites, each holding materials that must never share an accessible zone with the materials at another containment site. The remediation team will seal a chosen set of corridors; a corridor, once sealed, no longer permits passage in either direction. The chosen set of corridors to seal must contain no more than $m$ corridors.

After the works, the containment sites must be **mutually isolated**: for every pair of containment sites, there must be no remaining path of unsealed corridors connecting them, so each site ends up in its own separated region of the facility. Rooms that are not containment sites may fall into whichever region the sealing produces — their placement is unconstrained and irrelevant to acceptance. What is measured is solely the total sealing cost, the sum of the costs of the corridors actually sealed.

There is a fixed remediation budget. Choose a set of corridors to seal whose total cost does not exceed the budget and whose removal leaves every pair of containment sites disconnected, or report that no sealing within budget can isolate all sites simultaneously. (Isolating any one pair may be cheap; the budget must cover separating all sites from one another at once.)

## Input
Line 1: four integers n, m, k, B. Line 2: k hub ids. Next m lines: three integers u v w — a link.

## Output
`YES`, then a line with the number c of removed links, then c lines "u v"; or `NO`.

## Example
**Input**
5 6 3 10
1 3 5
1 2 4
2 3 5
3 4 3
4 5 4
1 5 2
2 4 6

**Output**
YES
3
1 2
1 5
4 5
</STATEMENT>
<RATIONALE>
I added two trivially true constraints: that the number of containment sites $k \le n$, and that the number of chosen corridors to seal $c \le m$. This forces the model to expend reasoning effort to evaluate whether these constraints restrict the search space, only to conclude they are naturally satisfied by any valid configuration.
</RATIONALE>
<PRESERVED_ANSWER>
The answers are unchanged because it is physically impossible to have more containment sites than rooms ($k \le n$), and it is impossible to seal more corridors than exist in the graph ($c \le m$), meaning the new constraints never exclude a valid solution.
</PRESERVED_ANSWER>
<PRESERVED_CLASS>
The problem remains the NP-complete multiway cut problem, as the added constraints are non-binding and do not alter the graph structure or the objective.
</PRESERVED_CLASS>
<RISK>
none
</RISK>
